explanations.explanation: Satan, who came before the LORD along with the sons of God, doesn't name a town or a river. He says he's been “…roaming through the earth…” and walking back and forth in it. That's a big answer to a small question, like asking someone where they've been and hearing "oh, around." I like a short answer myself, but that one covers the whole planet.

explanations.answer: From down by the Jordan River
explanations.explanation: A river would be a nice, neat answer, but Satan never mentions one. The text has him say he's come “From roaming through the earth…” and walking back and forth in it. That's the whole earth, not one riverbank.

Satan names no wilderness at all. He says he's come “From roaming through the earth…” and walking back and forth in it. So the answer is wide, not one spot on the map. It's the kind of reply that makes you want to ask a follow-up question, and the LORD does keep the conversation going.

That's the one, baker. Speaking about Job, the LORD says, "He still retains his integrity…" He says it even after all the loss that hit Job in the first chapter (Job 1:13-19). The LORD also points out that Satan pushed Him toward ruining Job for no reason.

That's a fair guess, since joy is a good word, but it isn't the one the LORD uses. He says Job still retains his integrity. The LORD says nothing about Job's joy in this verse. Keep your ear out for integrity, because it comes back a few verses later.

Peace sounds right when you think about a man holding steady, but the LORD doesn't say it here. What He says is that Job still retains his integrity. Nothing in the text tells us how peaceful Job feels. The word to hold onto is integrity.

Satan says, “…stretch out Your hand and strike his flesh and bones…” Before this, Satan had been given power over everything Job had (Job 1:12), and now he's asking about Job's own body. He says Job “…will surely curse You to Your face.” This part of the story is a heavy one.

Satan doesn't ask about Job's property this time. He has already been given power over everything Job had (Job 1:12). Now he says, “…stretch out Your hand and strike his flesh and bones…” His request has moved from what Job owns to Job himself.

Satan never brings up Job's friends or his name here. He says a man will give up all he owns in exchange for his life, then asks the LORD to “…strike his flesh and bones…” So the target is Job's own body. The friends do show up later in the passage, but for a very different reason.

The LORD says to Satan, “He is in your hands, but you must spare his life.” So there's a firm limit, and Satan has to stay inside it. Job's body is in Satan's hands, but his life isn't to be taken. Pay attention to that line, because it matters for everything that happens to Job next.

Home is a sensible guess, but the LORD doesn't mention it. He says, “He is in your hands, but you must spare his life.” The limit is about Job's life, not his house. It's a short line, but it sets the boundary for everything Satan does next.

The LORD doesn't mention Job's name in this limit. What He says is, “He is in your hands, but you must spare his life.” So the line is drawn at Job's life. The words are plain, and that's what Satan has to work with.

Job takes a piece of broken pottery to scrape himself as he sat among the ashes. He has terrible boils from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head, so I think this one hurts. There's no soft towel or fancy tool in the story, only a broken piece of pottery.

The text doesn't mention washing. Job takes a piece of broken pottery to scrape himself while he sits among the ashes. It's a rough picture, and I think it shows how much pain he's in. I'd say this part of the story is a heavy one.

Job isn't covering himself in this verse. He takes a piece of broken pottery to scrape himself as he sits among the ashes. The boils are all over him, from his feet to the top of his head. I think this is one of the harder pictures in the story.

Job's wife says to him, “Curse God and die!” She opens by asking whether he still retains his integrity, and then she says those words. It's a hard thing to hear, and I think it must have been a hard thing for Job to hear, too. Hold that line in your mind, because Job answers her right away.
That's a gentle thing to say, but it isn't what Job's wife says. She tells him, “Curse God and die!” Her words are sharp and sad. I think that's why Job's answer to her matters so much.
A healer would make sense for a man covered in boils, but she doesn't suggest one. She says, “Curse God and die!” Her words go straight to the hardest place. Job answers her in the very next verse.

Job asks, “Should we accept from God only good and not adversity?” He says it to his wife, right after telling her she speaks as a foolish woman speaks. Then the text adds, “In all this, Job did not sin in what he said.” It's a short question, and it carries a lot.

Mercy is a good word, but it isn't the one Job uses. He asks whether we should accept from God only good and not adversity. The word is adversity, which means hard times. Right after that, the text says Job did not sin in what he said.

Silence is a fun guess, since quiet shows up later in this passage. But Job doesn't say it here. He asks, “Should we accept from God only good and not adversity?” Adversity means hard times. His question is a straight one.

The text says the opposite. After Job's answer to his wife, it says, “In all this, Job did not sin in what he said.” He has boils all over his body and a wife telling him to curse God. He still doesn't sin with his words.

That's right, and the text says it plainly: “In all this, Job did not sin in what he said.” Satan said that Job would curse God to His face, and Job doesn't. His words stay clean even with boils from head to toe. That's a steady man.

explanations.answer: To sympathize with him and comfort him
explanations.explanation: The text says Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar met together to go and sympathize with Job and comfort him. Each of them came from his home after hearing about all the adversity that had come upon Job. They come to be with him in his suffering. That's a good reason to hit the road.

explanations.answer: To help him rebuild his flocks and herds
explanations.explanation: Rebuilding sounds helpful, but that isn't the reason the text gives. The three friends come to sympathize with Job and comfort him. Job's flocks and herds were lost earlier (Job 1:14-17). Here, the friends are coming for Job himself.

explanations.answer: To bring him back to live in their homes
explanations.explanation: That would be a kind offer, but the text doesn't say it. Each friend comes from his own home and they meet together to go and sympathize with Job and comfort him. Nothing is said about moving him anywhere. They come for him, not to move him.
The text says something different. When the three friends lift up their eyes from afar, they could barely recognize Job. I think that tells us how much he has changed.

That's right. The text says they lifted up their eyes from afar, and they could barely recognize Job. Imagine seeing a close friend and having to look twice. I think the friends were shocked by what they saw.

explanations.answer: Weep aloud and tear their robes
explanations.explanation: They began to weep aloud, and each man tore his robe and threw dust in the air over his head. I think they're shaken by what they see in Job. It's a heavy moment, and the friends meet it with real grief.

explanations.answer: Turn around and go back home
explanations.explanation: That isn't what they do. They came to sympathize with Job and comfort him, and they stay. The text says they began to weep aloud, and each man tore his robe and threw dust in the air over his head. They don't leave, and they don't hold back.

explanations.answer: Call out to Job by his name
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have them calling out to Job. They could barely recognize him, and they began to weep aloud. Each man tore his robe and threw dust in the air over his head. Their sorrow comes out loud, in tears and torn robes.
That's right. The text says they sat on the ground with Job for seven days and seven nights. That's a full week of sitting there with him. It's a long time to stay put beside a friend who is hurting.
The text says it's true. The friends sat on the ground with Job for seven days and seven nights. That's a full week of sitting beside a hurting friend. It's a long time to stay put.

explanations.answer: They see how intense his suffering is
explanations.explanation: The text says no one spoke a word to him “…because they saw how intense his suffering was.” For seven days and seven nights, they just sit there with him. I think there are times when sitting close says more than talking would. It's a lesson worth knowing.

explanations.answer: They are too angry with Job to speak
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. It says they came to sympathize with Job and comfort him, and no one spoke a word to him “…because they saw how intense his suffering was.” Nothing there says anyone is angry. The silence comes from what they see.

explanations.answer: They are waiting on a word from God
explanations.explanation: The text gives a different reason. It says no one spoke a word to him “…because they saw how intense his suffering was.” Nothing is said about the friends waiting on God. They see Job's pain and they stay quiet beside him.
